messages.author: 7c8d0f9d874c013e
messages.subject: Distance Sampling Stratification
parts:
Greetings. I have an analysis which I have recently completed in
Program Distance. I am converting it over to the package unmarked in
the hopes of using the results in a broader hierarchical analysis. So
far, I have been successful in producing consistent results for the
entire study area estimates.

In program distance I am using all samples to produce the detection
function, however I have 24 separate territories where I would like to
produce stratified density estimates. So far, in unmarked I haven't
seen an obvious way to do this. When I use predict, I do get 24
answers, but they are all identical.

Is there a particular way to set this up? One thought I had was to
include the territory ID as a covariate, then use backTranformation
and LinearComb to explore the results, but this doesn't seem right.

Any pointers would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

messages.author: 681fb59733e01a1e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Distance Sampling Stratification   - small-area estimation, estimating random effects, prediction in distance sampling
parts:
hi Rob,
 one possibility is you could use the 24 territories as a factor covariate -- but thats a lot of levels.  I guess maybe you need a random effect for this purpose to be most efficient, which we don't have, explicitly,
 Coincidentally, Richard just yesterday implemented a whole bunch of Best Unbiased prediction routines which will produce estimates of N[i] for each sample unit, including, I think, for distance sampling. He might allow you to test those functions.
 So while this doesn't build the random effects structure into the model (site or stratum effects) it allows you to produce estimates of N[i] (or density) for _each_ sample unit.
 
 Richard?
 
 BTW, I added a bunch of tags to the subject heading for people searching on this stuff in the future.
 
regards
andy

messages.author: 7c8d0f9d874c013e
messages.subject: Re: Distance Sampling Stratification - small-area estimation, estimating random effects, prediction in distance sampling
parts:
Andy, Richard,

Thanks for the feedback and for adding the additional search terms.

I have tried using a 24 factor covariate approach that I suggested to
represent my stratified samples, but the results did not work out. I
still received consistent answers for each of the 24 sample
locations.

I would be happy to try out the new routines that Richard has been
working on if they apply to distance sampling.

In the mean time I have made progress in extracting the bootstrap
sample data out of Program Distance to feed into my Hierarchical
models. It's a very cumbersome process, and likely very error prone,
but it has allowed me to make progress. I am still interested in a
more direct approach using unmarked.

Thank you for all of your hard work!

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Distance Sampling Stratification - small-area estimation, estimating random effects, prediction in distance sampling
parts:
Hi Rob,

I will send you a beta version of unmarked that includes a ranef() function to compute Best Unbiased Predictions (BUP) of abundance at each point (N_i). First I want to clarify something. When you say that results did not work out. What do you mean exactly? Did the model not converge when you included the factor with 24 levels? If it did converge, then predict is giving you the correct answer. It may be the case that your model doesn't suggest that there are differences in *expected* abundance among sites.

Richard

parts:
Richard,

Thank you.

When I included the factor covariate with 24 levels and ran distsamp,
it does converge. However, when I run predict, I get 24 identical
values for the density. As you suggest, it may be working without
recognition of any differences in abundance per site.

With the "alpha" version (0.95) of ranef(), I do get 24 different
values for the Mode. I am still in the process of evaluating the
results to compare back with my results from Program Distance. I'll
let you know.

-Rob
